narrative:
The model estimates you have a 10% chance of not passing your final year, which means you’re right at the line where the school requires extra support. This isn’t a verdict that you’ll definitely fail, but it’s a signal that a few key factors are nudging the risk higher than the school is comfortable with.

The single biggest reason the model is cautious is that you’ve never failed a class before. That’s actually a good sign—it means you’ve been able to keep up so far—but it also means the model has less evidence of how you bounce back from setbacks. Next in importance is why you chose this school: you picked it mainly for its reputation. Students who choose schools for the course content or because it’s close to home tend to have slightly smoother paths, so the model sees your choice as a small extra risk. Finally, your father’s education level is a factor. While your mother has a higher degree, your father’s secondary-school background is less common among students who pass without extra help, and the model treats that as a modest push toward needing support.

The good news is that none of these factors are deal-breakers. The school is simply asking you to take remedial courses so you can build a stronger buffer. Focus on the areas where the model sees room for improvement: use the extra study time to explore the course material more deeply, and lean on the support systems already in place—your family backing, internet access, and clear ambition for higher education. These strengths can easily outweigh the small risks the model has flagged.
